summary: Lays out the message exchange between two Network Control Programs needed to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol in RFC 123. It shows the server and user sides step by step. It was replaced by RFC 145, which corrected an error in it.

subtitle: A step-by-step interpretation of the NCP exchange for the Initial Connection Protocol.

tldr.problem: RFC 123 described the Initial Connection Protocol, and this note gives one interpretation of the Network Control Program messages needed to carry it out.
tldr.mechanism: It lays out a server and user NCP exchange: request a link, send 32 bits of data, close that link, and establish the links used for later communication.
tldr.outcome: RFC 127 updated RFC 123, was updated by RFC 151, and was obsoleted by RFC 145.

sections.title: A Reading of the Initial Connection Protocol
sections.content:
J. Postel describes his interpretation of the exchange between Network Control Programs (NCPs) needed to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol in RFC 123. The document presents the exchange as a two-column table, with one column for the server NCP and one for the user NCP.

The note says that symbols not explained in its table are defined in RFC 123.
sections.plainLanguage: This note shows the messages that each NCP sends during connection setup. It is an interpretation of RFC 123, not a separate detailed protocol specification.

sections.title: The NCP Message Exchange
sections.content:
The server NCP listens for a connection on L. The user NCP sends RTS, U, L, l; the server responds with STR, L, U, 32 and sends 32 bits of data in one message on link l. The user receives the data, whose value is S.

Both sides then send CLS. They exchange further STR and RTS messages, wait for the connections, and send ALL allocations. The table then shows data sent and received on link l. The note defines its subscripted symbols as links, message allocations, and bit allocations.
sections.plainLanguage: The table first shows the server sending 32 bits to the user, then both sides closing that link. They establish further links and allocations before exchanging data.

sections.title: How This Note Fits
sections.content:
RFC 127 is a comment that sets out one author's interpretation of the NCP exchange in RFC 123. The note points readers back to RFC 123 for the meanings of symbols it does not define.

The unit metadata says RFC 127 updated RFC 123, was later updated by RFC 151, and was obsoleted by RFC 145.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a step-by-step explanation of an earlier connection procedure. RFC 145 later obsoleted it.

references.text: RFC 123, which defines the Initial Connection Protocol and the symbols used here.
